question.text:
Which of the following integrals are equivalent to $\Gamma(z)$ for $\textrm{Re}(z) > 0?$

  1. $\displaystyle 2\int_0^\infty \dfrac{e^{-t^2}}{t^{2z-2}} \, \textrm dt$
  2. $\displaystyle 2\int_1^\infty \dfrac{t^{z}}{e^{t^2}} \, \textrm dt$
  3. $\displaystyle 2\int_0^\infty t^{2z-1} e^{-t^2} \, \textrm dt$
question.explanation:
First, let's recall the definition of the gamma function:

\[ \Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1} e^{-t} \, \textrm dt, \qquad \textrm{Re}(z) > 0. \]

With this definition in mind, let's consider each of the given integrals.

  • Integral I does not match the definition. The integrand $\dfrac{e^{-t^2}}{t^{2z-2}}$ is not equivalent to that shown in the definition.

  • Integral II does not match the definition. The lower bound of integration does not match that given in the definition.

  • Integral III matches the definition. We use a substitution $s=t^2,$ then $2 t \, \textrm dt = \textrm ds.$ We get \begin{align*} 2\int_0^\infty t^{2z-1} e^{-t^2} \, \textrm dt &= 2\int_0^\infty t^{2(z-1)+1} e^{-t^2} \, \textrm dt \\[3pt] &= \int_0^\infty t^{2(z-1)} e^{-t^2} (2t) \, \textrm dt \\[3pt] &= \int_0^\infty s^{z-1}e^{-s} \, \textrm ds = \Gamma(z). \end{align*}

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

exampleAnswers.title: Evaluating the Gamma Function at a Multiple of One-Half

question.explanation:
To evaluate the gamma function at multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

\[ \Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z), \qquad \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\pi} \]

So, we have the following:

\[\begin{align*} \Gamma \left( \dfrac{3}{2} \right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt\pi \\[5pt] \end{align*}\]

Therefore,

\[ \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) + \Gamma \left( \dfrac{3}{2} \right) = \sqrt\pi + \dfrac12\sqrt\pi = \dfrac32\sqrt\pi. \]

question.explanation:
To evaluate the gamma function at multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

\[ \Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z), \qquad \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\pi} \]

So, we have the following:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{16\sqrt{\pi}}{15} \,\Gamma \left( \dfrac{9}{2} \right) &= \dfrac{16\sqrt{\pi}}{15}\cdot \dfrac{7}{2} \cdot\Gamma \left( \dfrac{7}{2} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{16\sqrt{\pi}}{15}\cdot \dfrac{7}{2} \cdot \dfrac{5}{2} \Gamma \left( \dfrac{5}{2} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{16\sqrt{\pi}}{15}\cdot \dfrac{7}{2} \cdot \dfrac{5}{2} \cdot \dfrac{3}{2} \Gamma \left( \dfrac{3}{2} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{16\sqrt{\pi}}{15}\cdot \dfrac{7}{2} \cdot \dfrac{5}{2} \cdot \dfrac{3}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{16\sqrt{\pi}}{15} \cdot \dfrac{7}{2} \cdot \dfrac{5}{2} \cdot \dfrac{3}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{\pi} \\[5pt] &= 7\pi \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating the Gamma Function at a Multiple of One-Half

question.explanation:
To evaluate the gamma function at multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

\[ \Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z), \qquad \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\pi} \]

So, we have the following:

\[ \Gamma \left( \dfrac{3}{2} \right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt\pi, \]

\begin{align*} \Gamma \left( \dfrac{7}{2} \right) &= \dfrac{5}{2}\, \Gamma \left( \dfrac{5}{2} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{2} \cdot \dfrac{3}{2} \,\Gamma \left( \dfrac{3}{2} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{2} \cdot \dfrac{3}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt\pi\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{15}{8} \sqrt\pi \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \dfrac{4}{\sqrt\pi}\,\Gamma \left( \dfrac{7}{2} \right)+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt\pi}\,\Gamma \left( \dfrac{3}{2} \right) = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt\pi}\cdot \dfrac{15}{8} \sqrt\pi +\dfrac{1}{\sqrt\pi}\cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt\pi = 8 . \]

example.title: Evaluating the Gamma Function at a Multiple of One-Half

question.explanation:
To evaluate the gamma function at multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

\[ \Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z), \qquad \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\pi} \]

So, we have the following:

\[ \Gamma \left( \dfrac{5}{2} \right) = \dfrac{3}{2} \Gamma \left( \dfrac{3}{2} \right) = \dfrac{3}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \dfrac{3}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt\pi = \dfrac{3}{4} \sqrt\pi, \]

\begin{align*} \Gamma \left( \dfrac{7}{2} \right) = \dfrac{5}{2} \Gamma \left( \dfrac{5}{2} \right) = \dfrac{5}{2} \cdot \dfrac{3}{4} \sqrt\pi = \dfrac{15}{8} \sqrt\pi \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \dfrac{8}{3}\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma \left( \dfrac{7}{2} \right) + \dfrac{4}{3}\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma \left( \dfrac{5}{2} \right) = \dfrac{8}{3}\sqrt\pi\cdot \dfrac{15}{8} \sqrt\pi + \dfrac{4}{3}\sqrt\pi \cdot \dfrac{3}{4} \sqrt\pi = 6 \pi. \]
